div.p: Explaining prosocial behavior is a central goal in classic and contemporary behavioral science.

Here, for the first time, we apply modern machine learning techniques to uncover the full predictive potential that personality traits have for prosocial behavior. We utilize a large-scale dataset (N = 2,707; 81 personality traits) and state-of-the-art statistical models to predict an incentivized measure of prosocial behavior, Social Value Orientation (SVO). We conclude: (1) traits explain 13.9% of the variance in SVO; (2) linear models are sufficient to obtain good prediction; (3) trait-trait interactions do not improve prediction; (4) narrow traits improve prediction beyond basic personality (i.e., the HEXACO); ( 5) there is a moderate association between the univariate predictive power of a trait and its multivariate predictive power, suggesting that univariate estimates (e.g., Pearson's correlation) can serve as a useful proxy for multivariate variable importance. We propose that the limited usefulness of nonlinear models may stem from current measurement practices in personality science, which tend to favor linearly related constructs. Overall, our study provides a benchmark for how well personality predicts SVO and charts a course toward better prediction of prosocial behavior.

div.head: Plain language summary
div.p: The importance of being kind, helpful, and cooperative-of behaving prosocially-is undeniable. And yet, not everyone is equally prosocial. In fact, research in the social and behavioral sciences consistently shows that prosociality differs between individuals and is predicted by individuals' personalities. This research, however, typically only manages to explain a small portion of the variance in prosocial behavioral tendencies, rarely going beyond 9% (corresponding to a correlation of r = .30). One possible explanation for the lack of better prediction is the widespread use of constrained statistical models including only few personality traits as predictors at a time. Using a large set of predictors and state-of-the-art statistical models, we estimate that personality traits account for 13.9% of the variance in Social Value Orientation, an established indicator of prosocial behavior. By modeling multiple personality traits in tandem, we thereby break the 9% ceiling-a feat that single-predictor models rarely manage.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Prosocial behaviors (i.e., acts that benefit others) represent perhaps the brightest side of human nature. Individuals donate organs to strangers, nurture the young and the old, build tightly knit communities, and sacrifice their own wellbeing to protect the climate for future generations (Thielmann & Pfattheicher, 2022). However, not everyone is equally prosocial.

Previous research has documented extensive individual variation in the propensity to behave in prosocial ways (e.g., Fehr & Fischbacher, 2002;Hilbig et al., 2014;Murphy & Ackermann, 2014), spawning an impressive research endeavor into the personality basis of prosocial behavior (Thielmann et al., 2020). At the heart of this endeavor lies the goal of mapping personality traits onto prosocial behavior-or, stated differently, to predict prosocial behavior from personality. Critically, however, most personality predictors are limited in their explanatory power, accounting for less than 5% of the variance in prosocial behavior (Thielmann et al., 2020). In the present investigation, we explore whether applying machine learning techniques that account for potential nonlinear relations and make use of a large set of personality predictors can improve the predictive power of personality to answer the question "how much can personality predict prosocial behavior?". We do so by drawing on the specific example of Social Value Orientation (SVO) as an established indicator of prosocial behavioral tendencies (Balliet et al., 2009;McClintock & Liebrand, 1988;Murphy & Ackermann, 2014).

div.head: Beyond univariate prediction
div.p: Although prediction is a major goal in many scientific fields (Yarkoni & Westfall, 2017), the search for strong predictors plays a particularly prominent role in the history of the social sciences, especially in personality research (Mõttus et al., 2020). During the decades-old person-situation debate (Epstein & O'Brien, 1985;Pervin, 1989), personality research was heavily criticized for only accounting for (very) small portions of variance in certain outcomes, at best reaching 9% (or, equivalently, r = .30; Mischel, 1968). Consequently, some have argued that the study of personality traits should be abandoned altogether (Shweder, 1975). The debate was eventually resolved (see, e.g., Fleeson, 2004;Hogan, 2009;Kenrick & Funder, 1988), and personality science persevered-indeed, the use of personality measures spread to many fields within and beyond psychology, including sociology, behavioral economics, and medicine (e.g., Chapman et al., 2011;Turner, 1988). Even so, most effect sizes in personality research remain modest to this day (i.e., r < .30; Bosco et al., 2015;Funder & Ozer, 2019;Richard et al., 2003), and the case of personality and prosocial behavior is no different (i.e., the strongest predictor identified in the meta-analysis by Thielmann et al., 2020, attained 𝜌 ̂ = .26).

The apparent stability of this finding suggests that the predictive power of personality psychology hit a ceiling fifty years ago and never advanced beyond it. 1 But is this truly the upper bound of our ability to predict prosocial behavior via personality? Perhaps not. Most of the field has focused on univariate prediction, that is, using a single trait to predict behavior (Thielmann et al., 2020). Modern predictive models, by contrast, can leverage the unique contributions of hundreds (or thousands) of predictors at once. The disregard for multivariate prediction may have been limiting the predictive capabilities of the field. Indeed, a simulation study by Ahadi and Diener (1989) showed that if a behavior is determined by multiple traits, a single trait obtains an upper bound on its predictive capacity (e.g., a behavior determined by four traits has a limit of r = .45 for a single trait). Thus, a modern look at predicting behavior from personality demands going beyond univariate models.

div.head: Benchmarking personality and prosocial behavior
div.p: The question of how well personality predicts prosocial behavior is perhaps more pertinent than ever. Recently, multiple scholars have argued that prediction ought to be an important scientific goal on par with description and explanation (e.g., Mõttus et al., 2020;Yarkoni & Westfall, 2017). At the same time, the adoption of machine learning techniques has provided social and behavioral scientists with the tools to work rigorously toward better predictive models (Bleidorn & Hopwood, 2019;Rosenbusch et al., 2021). In particular, the practice of benchmarking-that is, evaluating statistical models based on their predictive performance on a welldefined task (typically an openly available dataset) and publishing the result for others to compare with or beat-has been highlighted as a central tool in securing a cumulative scientific endeavor (Rocca & Yarkoni, 2021).

We set out to provide the first benchmark of the personality-prosociality relation, essentially testing how much of the variance in prosocial behavior can be explained by personality in general. Answering such a question requires the use of machine learning techniques that are tailored to optimally make use of large datasets and account for the potentially complex relations between variables (Rosenbusch et al., 2021). If, for example, personality traits interact or are nonlinearly related to prosocial behavior, then a traditional linear model may underestimate the strength of the relation. However, adopting machine learning techniques substantially widens the space of choices the analyst must make. Thus, in addition to providing a benchmark of the field's ability to predict prosocial behavior, we chart a course toward better predictive models.

div.head: The present research: A case study on Social Value Orientation
div.p: There exists a plethora of measures of prosocial behavior, but for the present investigation we will focus on a single, widely used measure, namely SVO (Murphy et al., 2011).foot_2 An individual's SVO describes a relatively stable pattern in how they weigh the importance of their own outcome versus other people's outcomes and is typically measured using a series of resource-allocation decisions (Balliet et al., 2009;McClintock & Liebrand, 1988;Murphy & Ackermann, 2014). SVO shows strong ties to other measures of prosocial behavior, including economic game-like paradigms (Thielmann et al., 2020) as well as naturalistic, real-life measures (e.g., Cameron et al., 1998;Van Lange et al., 2007, 2011). Since SVO is measured using multiple decisions, it reflects individual differences more reliably than single-shot economic games (De Matos Fernandes et al., 2022;Murphy et al., 2011). Moreover, the SVO measure can be incentivized with actual money, rendering the decisions consequential. For these reasons, we take SVO as our outcome.

In a preregistered analysis, we apply 15 machine learning techniques to predict SVO from 81 personality predictors measured in the Prosocial Personality Project (PPP), a largescale project covering various personality traits and social behaviors. Specifically, we fitted a variety of linear models that attempt to select only the best personality predictors, two such linear models that included pairwise interactions between personality predictors, and four powerful nonlinear models. We thereby go beyond prior research, which has primarily dealt with univariate prediction and heavily constrained (i.e., linear) models, and provide a thorough benchmark of the relation between personality and SVO.

div.head: Sample
div.p: The Prosocial Personality Project. Our analyses rely on data from the PPP. The measures included in the PPP were chosen following an exhaustive meta-analysis summarizing six decades of research on personality and prosocial behavior in economic games (Thielmann et al., 2020), which was then extended by a thorough literature search for constructs related to prosociality and related constructs (for more details, see https://osf.io/m2abp/). Since the PPP arguably covers the breadth of known prosocial personality traits, we permit ourselves to make claims concerning this field of research as a whole and its present capacity for predicting SVO.

The PPP data were collected online over multiple measurement occasions between November 2019 and May 2023 via a panel provider in Germany. For the current investigation, we used data from waves T1-T5 as well as follow-up waves 2020-05b and 2021-10. Pre-specified exclusion criteria slightly varied from wave to wave, but generally included failing instructed attention checks, extremely low variance in responses, low response times, inconsistencies in demographic variables across waves, and multiple participation in one and the same wave.

Detailed information on sampling, exclusion criteria, payment, etc. is available on the Open Science Framework (OSF; https://osf.io/m2abp/). Data from the PPP has been used in prior publications, of which the full list is also available on the OSF (https://osf.io/8xhkd). Of these, one prior publication concerned SVO (Hilbig et al., 2023), but none have investigated the research question addressed here. Notably, Hilbig et al. (2023) only looked at univariate prediction.

Participants. Participants for the PPP were recruited via a German panel provider with the goal of obtaining a sample that is approximately representative of the German population with regard to age, gender, and educational level. The present investigation draws on all participants in the PPP which responded to wave T5 containing the SVO measure. The sample comprised 2,707 participants (1,286 identified as female, 1,419 as male, 2 had another gender identity) between 18 and 78 years (M = 43.2, SD = 12.5) with diverse educational backgrounds (942 held a degree from university, 766 from high school [German: Abitur], 967 from secondary school [German: Realschulabschluss], 28 from secondary general school [German:
Hauptschulabschluss], 1 none, 3 other) and employment statuses (1709 were employed, 223 independent, 85 unemployed, 234 retired, 115 homemaker, 273 student or apprenticeships, 68 other).

div.head: Analytic strategy
div.p: A brief introduction to nonlinear models. Nonlinear models allow researchers to uncover complex statistical relations in data that go beyond the linear constraint imposed by conventional statistical analyses. There exist a wide variety of nonlinear models, some of which work very differently from the linear model; for example, a random forest works by fitting thousands of decision trees (e.g., "if X1 is above 2.0 and X2 is below 1.5, predict that y equals 3.2") on bootstrap samples of the data and averaging their predictions (see James et al., 2013, for an introduction to many of the models considered here). One challenge that arises with such complex models is that they can pick up arbitrary noise in the dataset and thereby dramatically inflate the apparent accuracy of a model (known as overfitting; Rocca & Yarkoni, 2021). To counter this, one must evaluate models on different data than it is fitted to-a procedure known as cross-validation. In our case, we fitted the models on 70% of the dataset, and tested their predictions on the remaining 30%. An additional challenge is that many machine learning models contain so-called hyperparamters (or tuning parameters) which constrain or control the way they are fitted. For example, the random forest contains one hyperparameter specifying the number of decision trees, and another controlling the maximum number of branches per tree. The optimal choice of hyperparameters is unknown and must be determined by the analyst (Probst et al., 2019). To do so, one common approach is to perform a grid search, whereby many models are fitted across a range of hyperparameter values, and the best performing model is selected using cross-validation (Bischl et al., 2023).

Statistical models. We ran a plurality of statistical models. These can be grouped into three types: (1) linear additive models, (2) linear models including pairwise interaction terms obeying a strong hierarchy constraint, that is, where inclusion of an interaction effect implies inclusion of the main effects (Bien et al., 2013), and (3) nonlinear models. The full list of models and their respective hyperparameters is shown in Table 2.

[Table 2 goes here] Analytic strategy. First, the dataset was split 70:30 into a training set (n = 1,894) and a test set (n = 813) and all predictors were standardized based on the training set. The linear models and models with interactions were tuned with a grid search. The deep neural network was tuned using early stopping and a validation split of .20. All other nonlinear models were tuned using Bayesian model-based optimization running for 1,000 iterations (half as initial exploration). The optimal set of hyperparameters was identified using the 10-fold cross-validation MSE. After training, the models were evaluated on the test set. Specifically, we computed the R 2 , defined as 1 minus the ratio between the variance of the residuals and the total variance in the test data. To isolate the predictive power of a basic personality model (i.e., the HEXACO, the entire procedure was then repeated using only the HEXACO dimensions as predictors. 3 All models and results from tuning are available on the OSF (https://osf.io/zcdk8).

Variable importance. To quantify the relative importance of each trait for predicting SVO, we calculated permutation-based variable importance (Fisher et al., 2018). First, a trait variable is permuted, that is, the observations of the variable are shuffled around, thereby effectively turning it into noise. Next, a previously fitted model is used to predict SVO from the permuted variable. Variable importance is then calculated by dividing the permuted model's mean squared error (MSE) with the original (non-permuted) model's MSE. If the variable was important, the predictions from the permuted model should worsen (i.e., the MSE should increase), in turn yielding an importance score above 1. This procedure is repeated five times for each predictor and for each model.foot_4

Missing data. We included any participant having complete data on the SVO Slider in the analysis. Missing data (15% in total, mostly present in seven predictor variables coming from the same wave, i.e., follow-up 2021-10) was imputed via random forests. To estimate the level of uncertainty due to missingness, we imputed m = 5 datasets. Imputation was done separately on the train and test sets. The analysis was then conducted independently on each imputed dataset and the final estimates were pooled by averaging. Imputation diagnostics (i.e., trace lines and densities) are available on the OSF (https://osf.io/zcdk8).

Software. Most analyses were performed in R (R Core Team, 2021) and RStudio (RStudio Team, 2020). Missing data were imputed with mice (Buuren & Groothuis-Oudshoorn, 2011). Forward-backward selection was tuned with caret (Kuhn et al., 2022), relying on leaps (Miller, 2020). The lasso, ridge, relaxed lasso, and adaptive lasso regressions were fit using glmnet (Friedman et al., 2021). The elastic net was tuned with ensr (DeWitt & Bennett, 2019), also relying on glmnet. The SCAD and MCP models were fitted with ncvreg (Breheny, 2021), and the non-negative garrote with nnGarrote (Christidis et al., 2021). The models with interactions were fit with hierNet (Bien & Tibshirani, 2020) and glinternet (Lim & Hastie, 2015), respectively. Most nonlinear models were tuned using mlr3 (Lang et al., 2022), relying on xgboost (Chen et al., 2022), ranger for the random forest (Wright et al., 2022), and kernlab for the support vector regression (Karatzoglou et al., 2022). Variable importance measures were derived using iml (Molnar & Schratz, 2022), and the spline regression was fitted with segmented (Muggeo, 2023). The neural network was modelled using Python (Van Rossum & Drake, 2009), relying on keras (Chollet et al., 2015) for fitting and hyperopt (Bergstra et al., 2015) for tuning.

div.head: Deviations from preregistration
div.p: The analysis deviated from the preregistration in the following ways. Three deviations were made to improve the quality of the modeling: (1) the data were split 70:30, not 50:50, to make better use of the data for training, (2) the nonlinear models were tuned via model-based optimization instead of grid search to improve the chances of finding a global optimum within reasonable time, and (3) the support vector regression was additionally tuned for type of kernel (radial, polynomial) and polynomial degree. Finally, one deviation was made to reduce the model runtime to a manageable level: (4) the deep neural network was tuned using a validation split and early stopping instead of 10-fold cross-validation. The analyses of variable importance were not preregistered.

div.head: Personality traits can explain 13.9% of variance in SVO
div.p: Looking at Figure 1, the best-performing model (i.e., the deep neural network [DNN]) explained 13.9% of the variance in SVO. In other words, our results suggest that one seventh of SVO is attributable to personality traits. By contrast, the strongest univariate predictor, competitive jungle word view, explained 9.3% of the variance (see Table 1). This corresponds to a correlation of r = .31 and thus coincides with the r = .30 ceiling on prediction popularized by Mischel (1968). This comparison reveals that a substantial increase in predictive performance can be achieved by modeling multiple traits in tandem; indeed, multivariate models are able to clearly break the 9% ceiling. Although this analysis provides a snapshot of the present predictive capabilities of the field, it does not by itself tell us which direction the field should move towards to improve upon those predictions. For example, it may be that using more complex (e.g., nonlinear) models could better leverage the predictive potential of personality measures for prosocial behavior.
Alternatively, the answer may lie in developing better predictors. We turn to this matter next.

div.head: Linear models are sufficient
div.p: Linear models (e.g., Pearson's correlation) make extremely restrictive assumptions about the relation between variables, thereby potentially failing to adequately capture and leverage the (possibly nonlinear) pattern of the data. Even so, in our analyses, the best-performing linear model was able to attain an R 2 of 12.6%-only about one percentage point less than the best nonlinear model. This suggests that the effect of each predictor is mostly linear and thus wellmodelled by traditional means (see Oparina et al., 2022, for a similar conclusion in the context of wellbeing). Although these results remain to be generalized to measures beyond SVO, they suggest that researchers in the field of personality and prosocial behavior may rest assured that the currently dominant practice of using linear models is sufficient.

div.head: Interactions are not useful
div.p: Theoretically, there has been an interest in estimating trait-trait interactions (see Bauer & Shanahan, 2007;Vize et al., 2022). For instance, the "effect" of a given trait may be more pronounced in individuals having a particular level on another trait (i.e., a moderation effect).

We tested the utility of modeling interactions between personality traits using two models that attempt to select the best subset of predictors and their pairwise interactions. The best performing model with interactions explained 12.8% of the variance (Figure 1), showing that including interactions led to a miniscule improvement in prediction beyond the linear additive model, visible only at the third decimal. Moreover, the models including interactions introduced 41 and 66 interaction terms, respectively, thereby dramatically inflating the size of the model.foot_5

Taken together, modeling interactions between personality traits does not appear to be a fruitful approach for predicting SVO (see Vize et al., 2022, for a similar conclusion concerning the Big Five traits and a large set of life outcomes).foot_6

div.head: Narrow traits improve prediction
div.p: Figure 1 compares the predictive utility of a model trained only on the HEXACO personality model to the models trained on the entire predictor set (containing basic as well as narrow traits). The HEXACO is a basic personality model, developed to represent the entire personality space via six broad dimensions (Ashton & Lee, 2007). Notably, one of the six dimensions, Honesty-Humility, has previously been found to be a strong predictor of prosocial behavior in economic games (Thielmann et al., 2020). As shown, however, the models restricted to the HEXACO dimensions consistently performed about five percentage points worse than models leveraging the entire predictor set (Figure 1), suggesting that modeling multiple narrow traits in tandem yields incremental validity beyond the personality space spanned by the HEXACO dimensions.

Taken together, our results suggest that increasing model complexity (in terms of nonlinearities and interactions) matters less for good predictions than obtaining a comprehensive set of predictors (i.e., going beyond basic personality). In other words, the best way to attain better prediction is, at present, a matter of developing and discovering new and better traits (and measures thereof), rather than increasing the modeling complexity of the existing traits (see also Oparina et al., 2022). Therefore, we finally present two findings that may be useful in the search for better predictors.

div.head: Pearson's correlations are informative
div.p: Most work in the social sciences has focused on estimating linear univariate relations (Funder & Ozer, 2019;Thielmann et al., 2020), as often captured in a Pearson's correlation coefficient. This approach, however, may misrepresent the true importance of a predictor if the underlying reality is nonlinear and/or multivariate. Fortunately, permutation-based variable importance accounts for non-straightforward ways in which a predictor may influence prediction, such as via nonlinearities, interactions, or suppressor effectsfoot_7 -all of which are neglected by Pearson's correlation. Even so, Pearson's correlation may be an adequate measure of variable importance-especially if the relations at play are mostly linear, as implied by Figure 1. Indeed, as shown in Figure 2 for three exemplary models, the univariate R 2 value of each of the 81 personality predictors (roughly speaking, the square of Pearson's correlation) was moderately related to permutation-based importance measures derived from each model. In fact, when relating the two measures of variable importance using a spline regression (a type of linear regression where the regression line breaks at a "knot"), the univariate R 2 of the correlations explains between 19.0% and 63.4% of the variance in permutation-based importance, depending on the model. This shows that Pearson's correlation coefficient can approximate how important a personality trait is for predicting SVO, even when complexities are taken into consideration.

div.head: Correlations of at least .20 are important
div.p: Figure 2 reveals another interesting pattern; predictors that explain less than a certain proportion of variance in SVO on their own are of almost no importance in the models. That is, the line from the spline regression is almost completely horizontal before the "knot" value is reached. This pattern emerges in all models, although the exact position of the knot varies.

On average, the knot is located at R 2 = .051, suggesting that "useful" predictors tend to (univariately) explain at least 5.1% of the variance in SVO, corresponding to a Pearson's correlation of r = .23. 8 Thus, it seems that for a predictor to be important in the overall picture it must as a rule-of-thumb attain a Pearson's correlation of at least r = .20. Curiously, this result coincides with the mean effect size in 20 th century social and personality psychology (r = .21; Richard et al., 2003; see also Gignac & Szodorai, 2016). We suggest that this value also serves as a benchmark for researchers interested in the relation between personality and SVO. For instance, it may be used for power analyses when no better alternative to estimate the effect size is present (Lakens, 2022), and for evaluating the relative importance of the effect size of single predictors.

div.head: Discussion
div.p: Prosocial behavior is multiply determined by personality, situational factors, and their interaction (Furr & Funder, 2021;Li, 2023;Lewin, 1936). Given a specific situation (e.g., allocating money between oneself and a stranger), there are reliable individual differences that underlie prosociality (Thielmann et al., 2020). Continuing a long tradition in the social and behavioral sciences, we sought to thoroughly leverage the predictive potential of personality for a well-established measure of prosocial behavior, namely SVO. Using modern machine learning techniques that account for multivariate and nonlinear relations, we explained 13.9%

of the variance in SVO by personality traits, thus establishing a benchmark for the prediction of prosocial behavior based on stable dispositions. This multivariate benchmark breaks the well-known 9% (or r = .30) ceiling on univariate trait models of behavior. In addition, we found that the hitherto dominant practice of using linear models of trait-outcome relations (without interactions) is sufficient to achieve good prediction.

8 This was the only analysis we did not preregister. To ensure the result was not contingent on one specific analytic approach (see Multiverse analysis; Steegen et al., 2016), we applied multiple different models to validate the result. Specifically, we fitted a conditional inference tree, a spline regression, and a logistic regression. The resulting splits, knots, and inflection points were on average 0.044, 0.051, and 0.047, respectively (corresponding to a correlation coefficient between .21 and .23; for details, see the OSF: https://osf.io/zcdk8). The result thus appears robust to the type of analysis.

div.head: Rethinking benchmarks for personality and prosocial behavior
div.p: A crucial benefit of setting a benchmark is that it can serve as a reference point for what constitutes a good predictive model. Cohen (1988) provided three benchmarks for R 2 , namely 2% (small), 13% (medium), and 26% (large). In light of our 13.9% benchmark, these values may not be applicable to the field of personality and prosocial behavior. Given that the bestperforming model-containing no less than 81 predictors-attained no more than "medium" performance, the benchmarks provided by Cohen are clearly too optimistic for personality models of prosocial behavior (for similar reasoning on effects of personality, see Funder & Ozer, 2019;Gignac & Szodorai, 2016). In turn, any model explaining more than 13.9% of the variance in prosocial behavior (assuming the model is not cross-validated) is at risk of overfitting, that is, mistakenly including noise in the model, thereby modeling the data "too closely" (Rocca & Yarkoni, 2021).

This result also gives a new perspective on interpreting zero-order correlations. The strongest single predictor of SVO in the dataset (i.e., competitive jungle world view; Sibley & Duckitt, 2009) obtained a cross-validated R 2 of 9.3% (corresponding to a correlation of r = .31). By traditional rules-of-thumb (Cohen, 1988), this would constitute a "medium" effect size. Such a classification, however, is clearly misguided, as an optimal combination of 81 different traits only performs five percentage points better, corresponding to a correlation of r = .37. In this regard, and harking back to the notion of benchmarking, a single predictor explaining 9.3% can be considered an excellent predictor of prosocial behavior.

div.head: A multivariate perspective on broad and narrow traits
div.p: Personality science is populated with both broad and narrow trait constructs. Broad constructs (i.e., traits conceptualized within basic personality models, such as the Big Five and the HEXACO model; Goldberg, 1990;Ashton & Lee, 2007) seek to broadly capture the universe of potential personality traits while at the same time providing a parsimonious account of a variety of outcomes and phenomena. Narrower traits, in turn, may be tailored to specifically tap into the personality basis of a phenomenon and are thus expected to show better predictive utility (Ones & Viswesvaran, 1996). Our results showed that models fitted on all 81 traits available in our dataset clearly outperformed models fitted solely on the HEXACO dimensions.

Thus, although the HEXACO model arguably provides a parsimonious, yet relatively comprehensive, representation of the personality space, it misses out on some individual variation in prosocial behavior that only more fine-grained traits seem to capture (see also Paunonen et al., 2003;Seeboth & Mõttus, 2018;Speer et al., 2022; for similar findings spanning a wide range of outcomes). This finding differs from the meta-analysis by Thielmann et al. (2020) which found that both broad traits (e.g., the Honesty-Humility dimension of the HEXACO) and narrow traits (e.g., guilt proneness) performed similarly well as single predictors of prosocial behavior. This difference may stem from the fact that Thielmann et al. ( 2020) investigated univariate relations. That is, when considered in isolation, the predictive utilities of broad and narrow traits may be similar; when modelled in tandem, however, narrow traits show incrementally better predictive utility above and beyond basic personality.

div.head: Measuring to make the most of nonlinearities
div.p: Our results-and those of Oparina et al. ( 2022)-suggest that personality psychology benefits little from applying complex, nonlinear models. This stands in stark contrast to related fields, which have successfully applied nonlinear models to improve prediction (e.g., economics; Gogas & Papadimitriou, 2021;Nosratabadi et al., 2020). What could be holding personality psychology from reaping the same benefits of nonlinear modeling? Part of the answer may lie in the current measurement practices within personality science. When developing a novel scale, researchers are taught to strive for a symmetric distribution of responses with high variance (Clark & Watson, 1995) and to obtain large correlations with relevant criteria (Boateng et al., 2018;Devellis & Thorpe, 2021). In the context of nonlinear models, these practices have potential drawbacks. To obtain a symmetric distribution, researchers must avoid extreme items (e.g., "I often commit murder") which almost all participants answer in the same way (i.e., "strongly disagree"). However, such extreme responses may be the locus of nonlinearity because they capture true idiosyncrasies and deviations from typical behavioral patterns. Similarly, the emphasis on establishing criterion validity through (linear) correlations will naturally prioritize traits that tend to exhibit linear relations over those with nonlinear relations. As such, the current measurement practice may prioritize measures that are likely to display linear relations.

We conjecture that two extant approaches to measurement may be more amenable to nonlinear models. First, Mõttus et al. (2017Mõttus et al. ( , 2020) ) suggest to analyze psychometric scales at the item-level instead of (or in addition to) the construct-level. Individual item responses arguably tap into specific behavioral tendencies more accurately than trait scores aggregated across multiple items. As such, they may be more sensitive to context dependencies (i.e., interactions)

than aggregated trait scores. Prior work has shown this approach to be both reliable and predictive of relevant outcomes (Mõttus et al., 2017;Seeboth & Mõttus, 2018;Speer et al., 2022), albeit more demanding with regard to sample size (Revelle et al., 2021). Second, we join voices with scholars (e.g., Bleidorn and Hopwood, 2019;Mottus et al., 2020;Rauthmann, 2020) who suggest using objective measurements (e.g., digital traces; Stachl et al., 2020) as part of personality assessment. Such measures do not undergo any selection mechanism that potentially favor linear associations and could thus be leveraged better by nonlinear models.

div.head: Limitations
div.p: Before turning to the implications, some limitations of the current investigation must be acknowledged. First, the sample size (N = 2,707), albeit large for a psychological study, is relatively small compared to many machine learning applications (which sometimes contain millions of observations; e.g., Deng et al., 2009). This may adversely affect the performance of the nonlinear models as they sometimes require a large number of observations to learn the intricacies of the data. Second, although our results suggest that model complexity is not a particularly fruitful way to improve the prediction of SVO, we cannot rule out that more complex modeling techniques (e.g., ensembles) could improve upon prediction. Indeed, there are infinite ways to fit a model, and some will undoubtedly outperform ours. We thus invite the community to beat our 13.9% benchmark. 9

Third and finally, our conclusions rely on a single criterion, SVO, and may not generalize to other common measures of prosocial behavior. Indeed, the benchmarks we put forward should be interpreted as criterion-specific. However, the meta-analysis by Thielmann et al.
(2020) revealed SVO to be strongly correlated with prosocial behavior in all economic games that capture active prosociality (see also Balliet et al., 2009). In addition, SVO has been linked

to other indicators of real-life prosocial behavior, such as donating to noble causes ( Van Lange et al., 2007), volunteering (Van Lange et al., 2011), and performing pro-environmental actions (Cameron et al., 1998). We can only conjecture that our conclusion about the adequacy of linear models and Pearson's correlations will generalize to other measures of prosocial behavior. 10

As for other fields of research, the generalization is even less straightforward, and we do not claim our results to hold for all kinds of outcome variables (but see Oparina et al., 2022). Rather, we hope to see researchers become aware of the possibility of investigating nonlinearities and setting benchmarks in their own fields of research.

div.head: Implications
div.p: 9 We note that there is one circumstance in which the 13.9% benchmark is impossible to break, namely if the error inherent in the SVO slider measure (i.e., the irreducible error) accounts for the remaining unexplained variance. 10 Although the PPP contains measures of some economic games (e.g., trust game, dictator game), the sample sizes of these measures is much lower than that of SVO. Given that nonlinear models can require a very large number of observations, we thus decided to focus on SVO rather than economic games.

Our results can be of service to the field in multiple ways-methodologically, theoretically, and in application. First, the 13.9% benchmark can assist in model evaluation, that is, it will help researchers to answer the elusive question "how good is my model?". The benchmark also has implications for how much we emphasize personality traits in theoretical models and ascribe relevance to them in applied settings: It tells us that in a multivariate perspective, personality is substantially more predictive of behavior than is implied by single correlations (cf. Thielmann et al., 2020). In fact, the best single-trait model explained 9.3% of the variance in SVO-almost five percentage points less than the best multivariate model. Second, our findings regarding the adequacy of simple models (i.e., linear models, Pearson's correlation) support the mainstream statistical practice to consider linear effects of personality traits rather than nonlinearities and trait-trait interactions. Third, the finding that narrower traits out-predict basic personality should motivate researchers to map out more nuanced aspects of personality to complement basic personality dimensions in the prediction of prosocial behavior. In fact, our results suggest that the way toward better predictive models lies in improving our predictors (e.g., considering personality nuances; Seeboth & Mõttus, 2018) more so than in increasing the complexity of our statistical modeling practices. Importantly, however, in taking such a way forward, researchers should prevent introducing ever more construct inflation (Thielmann, Hilbig, & Zettler, 2022). Fourth, in the service of identifying relevant predictors, our contribution can inform power analysis decisions (Lakens, 2022): Because important traits tend to attain correlations of at least r = .20, sample size calculations should be set to detect effects of at least r = .20. That said, there are notable exceptions to this rule (e.g., right-wing authoritarianism;

see Table 1), and the association between a trait's (univariate) correlation and (multivariate) variable importance is only moderate. We suggest using r = .20 only as a rough rule of thumb in the absence of better justifications.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: Above all, we hope to have demonstrated the uses of machine learning and large-scale datasets in behavioral science (see also Bleidorn & Hopwood, 2019). As noted by Culkin (1967, p. 52), "we shape our tools, and thereafter our tools shape us." The same goes for statistical tools; machine learning can not only provide us with new answers to old questions but also point us to a myriad of exciting and novel research ventures. note.p: We note that two traits may (and often do) correlate above r = .30, especially if they share considerable conceptual overlap(Bainbridge et al.,
2022). Nonetheless, the relation between personality traits and behavioral measures of prosociality remains at a small-to-medium size.

SVO is often conceptualized as a disposition (e.g.,Murphy & Ackermann, 2014). However, the measure entails a series of choices and is, thus, also commonly used as a behavior (e.g.,Hilbig et al., 2023).

The HEXACO model extends the Big Five by a sixth basic trait dimension, titled Honesty-Humility, that captures proactive prosociality (seeAshton et al., 2014). For a detailed discussion regarding other differences between the two personality models (i.e., between Emotionality and Neuroticism, and between Agreeableness in the two models), seeThielmann, Moshagen, et al. (2022).

We relied on the R package iml(Molnar & Schratz, 2022) to compute variable importance. As such, we were unable to investigate variable importance in the deep neural network, which was fitted using python.
The number of included interaction terms varied depending on the imputation (glinternet: 36-66, hierNet: 44-97). The reported numbers are medians across imputations.

We refrained from considering higher-order interactions (i.e., three-way interactions, four-way interactions, etc.) in our analysis due to their limited use in the field. Although it is possible that such interactions could potentially increase the predictive capability of the models, higher-order interactions are unlikely to be strong if the lowerorder interactions are not (a phenomenon known as the sparsity principle;Li et al., 2006).

Suppressor effects arise when the inclusion of a covariate increases the overall model performance by removing outcome-irrelevant variance in another predictor. A variable can be an important suppressor without being correlated with the outcome(Pandey & Elliott, 2010).
